vignette:
For Sameer, the world shrank nine months ago, collapsing into the tight, terrifying confines of a four-block walk. Before that night, he took a quiet pride in his work. As a housekeeper for a downtown office building, he found a certain peace in the late hours, in the methodical act of bringing order to the day’s chaos. The hum of his floor buffer across the vast, empty lobby, the clean scent of ammonia, the satisfaction of seeing his reflection in a polished window—these were the markers of a job well done, of a life he and his wife, Priya, were building.

The walk from the last bus stop to his apartment had been routine. He usually listened to music, his mind already on the dinner Priya would have waiting. But that night, there was no music, only the sound of two sets of footsteps quickening behind him. He remembers the cold shock more than the pain. A sharp pressure against his neck, a voice that was both young and ragged spitting a demand for his wallet and phone. He remembers the rough scrape of the brick wall against his cheek as he was shoved, the smell of stale cigarettes, the glint of something metallic under the weak streetlight. He gave them everything without a word, his body frozen, his mind a blank white screen of terror. The entire event lasted less than a minute.

In the weeks that followed, Sameer told everyone, especially Priya, that he was fine. He was lucky. They didn’t hurt him, not really. But the man who returned to work was not the same one who had left. The quiet, empty building, once his sanctuary, became a labyrinth of potential threats. Every echo in the long, dark hallways was the sound of approaching footsteps. The sudden roar of the industrial vacuum made him flinch, his heart hammering against his ribs as if trying to escape. He started taking his breaks inside a locked supply closet, the cramped space feeling safer than the cavernous, glass-walled offices.

At home, the change was more profound. He stopped taking the bus, insisting that Priya drive across town to pick him up after his shift, a request that strained their budget and her patience. He’d sit silently in the passenger seat on the way home, his head on a constant swivel, his eyes scanning every alley and doorway. He used to love cooking with Priya, the easy rhythm of their movements in the small kitchen. Now, he’d just sit at the table, staring at nothing, lost in a loop of the glinting metal and the rough voice. When she tried to touch him, to hold him at night, his body would go rigid. The nightmares were relentless—not of the robbery itself, but of being chased down endless, identical office corridors, the doors always locked. He’d wake up drenched in sweat, his own ragged breathing filling the silent bedroom.

He feels a gnawing shame that he can’t articulate. He sees himself as weak, a man who couldn’t protect the little he had. He replays the moment over and over, imagining different outcomes where he fought back, where he was brave. But the fantasy always dissolves into the humiliating reality of his own paralysis. The world he once saw as mostly good, a place of opportunity, now feels fundamentally unsafe. He is a ghost in his own life, polishing surfaces and emptying trash cans, while inside, the mess of that single minute remains, untouched and spreading.
